Below is a practical, evidence‑backed comparison of digital skills for the general workforce versus digital skills for tech jobs. I first define baseline digital skills, then contrast scope, competencies, tools/workflows, and how people use them at work, and finally give upskilling guidance and common pitfalls.

What “digital skills” mean in the general workforce
- Baseline definition and categories: Authoritative frameworks describe digital skills as the capability to use technology to solve problems and perform complex tasks in technology‑rich settings; widely referenced categories include information/data literacy, communication and collaboration, content creation, safety, and problem solving, often with proficiency levels from basic to advanced <cite id="38bdf598-0">Digital skills frameworks converge on five competency areas: information/data literacy, communication/collaboration, content creation, safety, and problem solving, with multiple proficiency levels, and are referenced by ITU, UNESCAP, OECD, and the European Commission</cite> <cite id="38bdf598-1">OECD frames digital skills as capability to use technology to resolve problems and perform complex tasks, and classifies workplace digital skills into clusters such as information processing, technical, transversal, and foundational; DigComp emphasizes information, communication, content creation, safety, and problem solving</cite> <cite id="38bdf598-2">Foundational models group digital skills into operational/technical abilities and higher‑order skills (information, communication, content creation, strategic), noting that information and strategic skills are the most problematic and can widen divides</cite>.
- What this looks like day‑to‑day: For non‑tech workers, fluency with office suites, collaboration platforms, email/communication suites, and basic troubleshooting; locating, evaluating, and synthesizing online information; creating documents/presentations; protecting privacy and security; and collaborating across tools; all oriented to getting work done and communicating effectively in technology‑mediated workflows <cite id="38bdf598-0">Information and data literacy, communication/collaboration, content creation, safety, and problem solving together span routine workplace tasks like finding, evaluating, sharing, and producing content digitally</cite> <cite id="38bdf598-1">Workplace‑oriented taxonomies emphasize information processing, technical operations, cross‑cutting transversal skills, and foundational device literacy</cite>.
- Measuring levels: Cross‑national adult assessments often operationalize “digital skills” as problem‑solving in technology‑rich environments rather than “computer literacy,” reflecting the ability to plan, target, and evaluate solutions across tasks <cite id="38bdf598-1">OECD’s adult learning study operationalizes digital skills as problem‑solving in technology‑rich settings, capturing complex task performance</cite>.

What “digital skills” mean in tech jobs
- Deeper specialization and higher abstraction: Tech roles build on the general foundations but require depth in specific problem spaces (algorithms, distributed systems, data/AI, security) and fluency with professional toolchains. Software engineering job profiles from major vendors and EU consortia enumerate competencies per role (developer, tester, architect, designer, PM) to support daily tasks, reflecting a layered skill stack beyond device/operational knowledge <cite id="aa7d1378-0">Career Space (BT, Cisco, IBM, Microsoft, Nokia, Siemens) defined job profiles (developer, tester, architect, designer, team lead, project manager, R&D director) and competencies per profile to cover software engineering tasks</cite>.
- Technical, analytical, and social-emotional triad in coding roles: Developers need (i) technical competencies in languages, libraries, platforms, version control, testing, and debugging; (ii) analytical competencies in problem decomposition, algorithmic reasoning, planning, and evaluation; and (iii) social-emotional competencies in communication, documentation, collaboration, and working independently and in groups—often as critical as operational “button‑knowledge” <cite id="aa7d1378-1">Software developer competencies span technical (theoretical background, community practices, interaction with systems), analytical (information analysis, problem solving, decision making), and social/emotional (communication, documentation, teamwork, pressure/failure handling)</cite>.
- Gaps at entry and on‑the‑job learning: Novices frequently struggle with collaboration/communication, source code control, and testing; many skills are learned on‑the‑job, signaling a mismatch between university exit profiles and workplace expectations and underscoring the need for experiential learning and mentorship <cite id="aa7d1378-2">New software graduates often lack productivity‑level skills in source code control and testing; communication and teamwork remain persistent gaps; developers learn many skills on‑the‑job, reflecting industry–university mismatches</cite>.

Data and AI roles (analytics/science/engineering)
- Core competencies and tool fluency: Organizations expect analysts to process business data, communicate insights, and use tools like Python, SQL, R, Tableau/Power BI, and cloud data platforms (BigQuery, Spark, Redshift), with familiarity scaling as data grows; the distinction between “analyst” and “scientist” deepens at advanced predictive/prescriptive analytics and unstructured data modeling, typically requiring stronger education and cross‑disciplinary knowledge (behavioral/social sciences, industrial engineering, computer science) <cite id="8c2f3ba3-0">Data literacy for analysts includes gathering/organizing data and performing prediction, trend analysis, and recommendations; tool fluency spans Python, SQL, R, Tableau/Power BI, and distributed platforms (BigQuery, Spark, Redshift); data scientists specialize in complex mining, modeling unstructured data, and advanced analytics with broader educational background</cite>.
- Competency models and job ads: Unified competency themes include organizational, technical analytical, ethical/regulatory, and cognitive/social skills; job‑ad analyses show employers prioritize communication, teamwork, problem solving, Python, English, and SQL, with a push toward multidisciplinary profiles—indicating that “data” jobs blend technical toolchains with business storytelling and governance <cite id="8c2f3ba3-1">Data science competency models group skills into organizational, technical analytical, ethical/regulatory, and cognitive/social themes; job ad analyses find top competencies are communication, teamwork, problem solving, Python, English, SQL, and emphasize multidisciplinary profiles</cite>.
- Market signals and certifications: Predictive dashboards for sustainable skills management indicate demand for data scientist roles followed by data analyst/data engineer; certifications (IBM/Azure) and required skill clusters (machine learning, statistics, data visualization) reflect current market expectations, with cloud credentials (AWS/GCP) highly desired alongside programming frameworks <cite id="8c2f3ba3-2">Market analyses recommend data scientist as top role, followed by analyst and engineer; certifications like IBM Data Science Professional and cloud platforms (AWS, GCP) are highly desired; required technical skills cluster in machine learning, statistics, and data visualization</cite>.

Cybersecurity and infrastructure roles
- Workforce competency frameworks: The U.S. Cybersecurity Competency Model (ETA/NICE/OPM) defines skill and knowledge requirements to improve organizational security posture, integrating competencies for cybersecurity professionals and related occupations (infrastructure operations, network defense, incident response); employers’ scenarios map directly to these competencies <cite id="7e554e5e-0">The Cybersecurity Competency Model (ETA, DHS, NICE) defines skill/knowledge needs to improve security posture, complementing the NICE framework and mapping employer scenarios to competencies</cite>.
- From competencies to readiness: Organizations increasingly recognize that documenting competencies is not the same as ensuring workforce readiness; competency lifecycle approaches add certification, evaluation, and training design to move people from “knowing” to performing reliably under pressure, including leadership roles <cite id="7e554e5e-1">Competence is not readiness; workforce readiness programs add certification, evaluation, and training design to build performance readiness, drawing on frameworks from OPM/NICE and leadership models</cite>.
- Entry points and assessments: Widely used certifications (e.g., CISSP) assess both technical and managerial expertise across domains like cryptography, network security, penetration testing, and compliance, providing standardized yardsticks for technical depth and governance awareness <cite id="7e554e5e-2">CISSP evaluates technical and managerial competence across cybersecurity domains; CyberMetric benchmarks assess knowledge across cryptography, network security, penetration testing, and compliance</cite>.

How general‑workforce digital skills differ from tech‑job digital skills
- Scope and abstraction
  - General workforce: Breadth over depth; tasks like finding, evaluating, and synthesizing information; collaborating across platforms; creating documents/presentations; protecting privacy; and solving everyday tech‑mediated problems; emphasis on safe, effective participation and communication <cite id="38bdf598-0">Digital competence spans information/data literacy, communication/collaboration, content creation, safety, and problem solving with proficiency levels</cite> <cite id="38bdf598-2">Operational/technical skills are necessary, but information and strategic skills are decisive for real‑world use</cite>.
  - Tech jobs: Depth in specific domains plus systems thinking; software engineers combine language/libraries/platform fluency with algorithmic/design/ops depth and social‑emotional collaboration; data/AI roles blend technical toolchains (SQL/Python, ML) with analytics storytelling and governance; cybersecurity roles require layered security, operations, and incident response competencies mapped to formal frameworks <cite id="aa7d1378-1">Developer competencies combine technical, analytical, and social-emotional dimensions</cite> <cite id="8c2f3ba3-0">Analysts and scientists differ in predictive/prescriptive analytics and unstructured data modeling, often requiring advanced education</cite> <cite id="7e554e5e-0">Cybersecurity competency models define skills for infrastructure operations, network defense, and assurance</cite>.
- Tools and workflows
  - General workforce: Office suites, collaboration platforms, email, browsers, basic troubleshooting; ad‑hoc queries and reports; secure communication; compliance with basic policies <cite id="38bdf598-1">Workplace digital skills clusters include information processing, technical operations, transversal collaboration, and foundational device literacy</cite>.
  - Tech jobs: Version control (code and data), CI/CD pipelines, testing frameworks, cloud platforms and databases (SQL/NoSQL), distributed data processing (Spark), data visualization/reporting, security tooling (IDS/IPS, SIEM), threat modeling, incident response playbooks, and compliance frameworks—often orchestrated across teams and environments <cite id="aa7d1378-0">Job profiles enumerate competencies tied to daily engineering tasks across roles</cite> <cite id="8c2f3ba3-0">Data roles require Python/SQL/visualization and distributed data platforms; scientists engage advanced modeling and unstructured data</cite> <cite id="7e554e5e-0">Network defense and incident response competencies are core to cybersecurity workflows</cite>.
- Problem types and outcomes
  - General workforce: Efficiency and communication—producing accurate artifacts, automating routine tasks, and collaborating securely across tools <cite id="38bdf598-0">Problem solving and communication/collaboration underpin workplace digital performance</cite>.
  - Tech jobs: System behavior and risk—designing robust, scalable, secure solutions; analyzing data to predict/prescribe actions; defending assets and responding to threats; often with quantifiable impact on reliability, latency, cost, accuracy, and risk exposure <cite id="aa7d1378-1">Analytical competencies include decomposition, logical/mathematical reasoning, and planning/evaluation</cite> <cite id="8c2f3ba3-0">Data scientists design modeling processes for unstructured data and advanced analytics</cite> <cite id="7e554e5e-1">Workforce readiness programs operationalize moving from competence to performance under pressure</cite>.

Shared skills and the bridge from general to tech
- Transferable foundations: Across roles, information literacy (evaluating sources), communication/collaboration, basic coding/data manipulation, and safe/ethical use of tools are transferable; general‑workforce training can scaffold readiness for tech paths by embedding problem‑solving practice, documentation, and safe experimentation <cite id="38bdf598-2">Information and strategic digital skills are the most problematic gaps and critical to equitable adoption</cite> <cite id="38bdf598-1">Digital skills frameworks emphasize information, communication, content creation, safety, and problem solving as transferable pillars</cite>.
- Coding and data literacy as bridge skills: Exposure to Python/SQL, version control (Git), and simple data workflows enables lateral moves into software/data roles; job‑market analyses repeatedly list Python, SQL, and communication/problem solving among top desired competencies alongside education, underscoring that “do‑able” projects and portfolio artifacts accelerate transitions <cite id="8c2f3ba3-1">Top competencies from job ads include communication, teamwork, problem solving, Python, English, SQL, with emphasis on multidisciplinary profiles</cite>.
- Security hygiene for everyone: General workforce benefits from basic cybersecurity practices (phishing awareness, strong auth, least privilege, secure collaboration), which reduce risk surfaces as organizations adopt AI and cloud—skills aligned with the broader security competency landscape and governance themes <cite id="7e554e5e-1">Security competencies and readiness require moving beyond lists to evaluation and effective training</cite> <cite id="8c2f3ba3-1">Ethical and regulatory competencies are core themes in data science competency models</cite>.

Common pitfalls and how to avoid them
- Mismatched expectations and over‑specialization: Universities and employers often misalign on early‑career readiness; communication, teamwork, and testing are persistent gaps—use project‑based learning, code reviews, and real data problems to close the loop <cite id="aa7d1378-2">Novice productivity gaps center on collaboration/communication and code control/testing; many skills are learned on‑the‑job</cite>.
- Neglecting soft skills in technical roles: Technical fluency without effective communication and documentation impairs delivery and adoption; integrate design/UX thinking, stakeholder mapping, and plain‑language communication into developer and data workflows <cite id="aa7d1378-1">Social and emotional competencies (communication, documentation, teamwork) are as critical as technical ones</cite> <cite id="8c2f3ba3-0">Data literacy must include efficiently communicating results to relevant parties</cite>.
- Relying on titles over competencies: Job‑ad analyses show employers value Python/SQL and soft skills as much as degrees; assess via scenario‑based tasks, kata‑style coding challenges, and live data projects, not just exams <cite id="8c2f3ba3-1">Employers prioritize communication, teamwork, problem solving, Python, English, SQL; companies often care less about degree and more about competencies</cite> <cite id="7e554e5e-0">Scenario‑based assessments map directly to employer‑identified competencies</cite>.

Practical upskilling pathways
- From general to developer/data paths:
  - 6–12 months: Master information‑to‑insight workflows—Python fundamentals, SQL querying, Git basics, small web app or dashboard with Streamlit/Power BI, and a public dataset project; weekly code reviews and pair‑learning to build communication/testing muscles <cite id="38bdf598-2">Strategic and information skills are the toughest divides; targeted practice improves equitable adoption</cite> <cite id="aa7d1378-2">Communication and testing are persistent gaps to address early</cite>.
  - 6–12+ months: Deepen systems/data—REST APIs, databases, CI/CD basics, data pipelines with cloud services, and medium‑sized ML project with evaluation/feedback loops; join open‑source communities to practice design/documentation and code quality <cite id="8c2f3ba3-0">Cloud platforms and distributed processing are expected competencies for analysts; scientists require deeper modeling and education</cite>.
- From general to cybersecurity path:
  - 12+ months: Network basics (TCP/IP, routing/switching), scripting for ops, and security concepts (cryptography, access control); pursue foundational certs (e.g., CompTIA Security+) and contribute to open source security tools or phishing awareness programs to build applied experience <cite id="7e554e5e-0">Competency models span infrastructure operations and network defense with scenario‑based mapping</cite> <cite id="7e554e5e-2">CISSP and CyberMetric benchmarks define technical domains and assess knowledge</cite>.
- Across all tech transitions:
  - Use competency frameworks (DigComp for baseline, SFIA/NICE/CISSP for domain specialization) to make explicit learning plans and track readiness; convert goals into measurable tasks (repo with tests, dashboard with governance notes, incident simulation write‑up) <cite id="38bdf598-0">DigComp provides proficiency levels across core areas to benchmark progress</cite> <cite id="8c2f3ba3-1">SFIA offers holistic ICT competency framing; job‑ad analyses guide current tool/soft skill emphasis</cite> <cite id="7e554e5e-0">NICE/ETA models tie competencies to concrete security scenarios</cite>.

Bottom line
- General workforce digital skills are about safe, effective participation and problem solving across everyday tools and processes; they emphasize information literacy, communication/collaboration, basic creation, and security hygiene in technology‑rich environments <cite id="38bdf598-0">Digital competence categories align to routine workplace tasks across information, communication, creation, safety, and problem solving</cite> <cite id="38bdf598-1">OECD defines digital skills as capability to use technology to resolve problems and perform complex tasks</cite>.
- Tech jobs build on these foundations to deliver at scale: software engineers orchestrate code, testing, and CI/CD; data/AI practitioners wrangle data, model, and communicate insights with governance; cybersecurity professionals design, monitor, and respond across infrastructure and threats—each with formal competency and readiness pathways <cite id="aa7d1378-0">Role‑specific competency lists from major IT vendors operationalize daily engineering tasks</cite> <cite id="8c2f3ba3-0">Analysts and scientists differ in predictive/prescriptive analytics and unstructured data modeling with higher educational depth</cite> <cite id="7e554e5e-0">Cybersecurity competency models govern infrastructure operations and defense competencies</cite>.
- In practice, bridge transferable skills to domain‑specific toolchains, emphasize communication/testing/documentation, and validate learning with realistic tasks and recognized frameworks to ensure readiness, not just competence <cite id="aa7d1378-2">Employers observe persistent gaps in communication, teamwork, code control, and testing at entry</cite> <cite id="8c2f3ba3-1">Job ads prioritize communication, problem solving, Python, and SQL over degrees</cite> <cite id="7e554e5e-1">Competence ≠ readiness; structured certification and assessment build reliable performance</cite>.

Title: Cognitive Software Engineering: A Research Framework and Roadmap
Snippet: In order to be able to analyze CASE tools, we first need to establish a list of the Software Engineering daily tasks and competencies. For this aim, we considered two data sources. For that, the consortium first determined a set of professional job profiles and then determined the required set of competencies for every profile. The competencies of the Career Space are listed in [1]. Our list of competencies is presented in Table 1. As the reader may notice, the list does not contain general skills of project management or quality assurance. That is because the original list of the Career Space contains project management and quality assurance skills that are specific to IT and Software Engineering. This perfectly fits our objective in the present research. Title: Computational Practices, Educational Theories, and Learning Development
Snippet: Competencies (which also in this paper include skills, as described and defined by other authors) needed by a software developer can be detailed through nine different elements or processes (identified in, for example, Ahmed, et al. 2013;Surakka and Malmi 2004) on what might be regarded as "soft skills", without emphasising skills regarded as operational or technical (manipulative and mechanical, for example). SkillScan (2012) takes an alternative approach, categorising competencies as: relationship; communication; management/leadership; analytical; creative; and physical or technical. For this paper, the competencies are broadly categorised into three different groups, formed from a coalescence of these sources: technical competencies (having a good understanding of the theoretical background of the field as well as common practices used and discussed by the community, including those enabling effective interactions between the individual with physical objects such as machines and technological systems); analytical competencies (abilities to collect and analyse information, problem-solve, and make decisions concerned with logical thinking, mathematical reasoning, and structural reasoning and planning); social and emotional competencies (effective communication skills when communicating with team members, customers, or team leaders, writing and understanding documentation such as manuals, tutorials, or trouble-shooting guides, being willing and able to share knowledge and expertise with fellow team members, working independently and within groups, analysing user needs and having a solid understanding of a company's needs, scrutinising information given, anticipating events that are hard to predict, and handling pressure and failure). Some competencies listed above are more obviously critical requirements, often easier to assess. Some are more related to short-term success, and those would be expected to be in high demand in job advertisements. Some competencies are more subtle, and related more to long-term success. Interestingly, these competencies relate strongly to those identified within school computing curricula. How school practices enable development towards these competency goals is our concern in this paper. 

Taking the range of required competencies (considered in the next section of the paper), our framework for analysis is shown in table 1. using this framework, we consider whether each selected learning theory can underpin the creation of learning activities required to develop each of these competency sets.

Title: Employers' Needs for Computer Science, Information Technology and Software Engineering Skills Among New Graduates
Snippet: Immediately after graduation, students in computer science typically struggle with becoming productive as software developers. Common difficulties reported by novice professionals include weaknesses in soft skills such as collaboration and communication, as well as in technical skills related to source code control and testing [1]. Direct observation of developers has confirmed that these skills play a large role in daily work and present substantial challenges [2]. Surveys further have revealed that developers learn many such skills on the job, reflecting gaps between skill upon graduation and respective accumulated skill thereafter [3,4]. 

What developers perceive about their strengths and weaknesses may differ from those perceived by other stakeholders, such as the educators who train them. For example, one study of the software industry in Philippines revealed a significant disconnect between the perceptions of workers about their weak human relations and collaboration skills (particularly leadership), versus perceptions of educators [5]. 

Studies of employers' perceptions of recent graduates' skills can help reveal weaknesses that potentially impact worker productivity. One literature review of empirical studies since 1995 revealed many such gaps between industry expectations and the abilities of graduates, the most significant of which were related to communication, teamwork, problem solving, testing and programming [6]. Exploring specific papers from that period provides more detailed insight into topical gaps. 

Several recurring themes appear among the literature cited above, the most prominent of which appears to be collaboration and communication, and another of which is software testing. Universities can train future software developers in such skills within the context of courses on computer science, software engineering, and information technology. Hence, ongoing research can inform the development of university curricula in two ways. 

First, studies can aid in updating the list of specific topics requiring attention. For instance, a paper based on a 1998 survey included a list of 25 "least important" topics for academia to focus on further emphasizing, two of which were artificial intelligence and robotics [7]. In the nearly two decades since the survey, both areas of expertise have grown in importance, leaping to the forefront of technological innovation and commercial development, with potentially transformative effects on the culture and economy [8]. Likewise, the papers cited above have little or no mention of big data, cloud computing, mobile app development or other new solution domains that may have become important to employers. Skill lists need continual refreshing based on fresh empirical studies.

Title: Data Swagger: A Systemic Approach to Train, Motivate and Engage Data Savvy Employees
Snippet: Data literacy is key to successful digital transformation and globalization. However, data competency demands are contextual to one's role in an organization. This study recognizes the differences between the definition of data literacy among two groups: data analysts/scientists and end-users. First, data analysts are responsible for processing data into valuable information for end-users. The results of these analyses must then be understood by end-users for them to make data-driven decisions with the highest possibility of success. For data analysts, data literacy involves competencies related to data science from gathering and organizing data to engaging in analyses like prediction, trend analysis, and recommendation development [13] [14]. Knowing how to effectively utilize different programs and applications like Python, SQL, R, Tableau and Microsoft PowerBI is becoming a key component of data literacy for data analysts. Working with bigger and more complex data also requires familiarity with tools that allow for easier collection, processing, and interpretation. For example, technologies such as Google BigQuery, Apache Spark, and AWS Redshift allow analysts to access, organize, and analyze large amounts of data. More importantly, literacy in data analytics must include competencies related to efficiently and effectively communicating results insights from data analyses with the relevant parties. 

The level of literacy in data science is what differentiates data analysts from data scientists in modern organizations. While data analysts play a significant role in helping businesses process structured business data and report on current trends, data scientists focus on complex data mining for advanced predictive and prescriptive analytics. Data scientists also specialize in designing data modeling processes that extract insight from unstructured data. Data literacy at this level involves competencies associated with behavioral and social sciences, industrial engineering, computer science, and advanced visualization and representation [8] [15]. For example, data scientists are familiar with the level of sophistication involved in big data processing and automation frameworks [16]. In addition to industry knowledge, a strong educational background is usually required to develop the depth of knowledge necessary to be a data scientist. 

At the end-user level, data literacy is associated with non-specialists who utilize extracted data to make informed decisions. Promoting data literacy amongst all employees enhances an organization's capacity to understand the value of data and make data-driven decisions.

Data literacy is key to successful digital transformation and globalization. However, data competency demands are contextual to one's role in an organization. This study recognizes the differences between the definition of data literacy among two groups: data analysts/scientists and end-users. First, data analysts are responsible for processing data into valuable information for end-users. The results of these analyses must then be understood by end-users for them to make data-driven decisions with the highest possibility of success. For data analysts, data literacy involves competencies related to data science from gathering and organizing data to engaging in analyses like prediction, trend analysis, and recommendation development [13] [14]. Knowing how to effectively utilize different programs and applications like Python, SQL, R, Tableau and Microsoft PowerBI is becoming a key component of data literacy for data analysts. Working with bigger and more complex data also requires familiarity with tools that allow for easier collection, processing, and interpretation. For example, technologies such as Google BigQuery, Apache Spark, and AWS Redshift allow analysts to access, organize, and analyze large amounts of data. More importantly, literacy in data analytics must include competencies related to efficiently and effectively communicating results insights from data analyses with the relevant parties. 

The level of literacy in data science is what differentiates data analysts from data scientists in modern organizations. While data analysts play a significant role in helping businesses process structured business data and report on current trends, data scientists focus on complex data mining for advanced predictive and prescriptive analytics. Data scientists also specialize in designing data modeling processes that extract insight from unstructured data. Data literacy at this level involves competencies associated with behavioral and social sciences, industrial engineering, computer science, and advanced visualization and representation [8] [15]. For example, data scientists are familiar with the level of sophistication involved in big data processing and automation frameworks [16]. In addition to industry knowledge, a strong educational background is usually required to develop the depth of knowledge necessary to be a data scientist. 

At the end-user level, data literacy is associated with non-specialists who utilize extracted data to make informed decisions. Promoting data literacy amongst all employees enhances an organization's capacity to understand the value of data and make data-driven decisions.

Title: Competency Lifecycle Roadmap: Toward Performance Readiness
Snippet: For the past several years, the CERT Program has helped client organizations improve their training and development programs. Several of these engagements focused on identifying and documenting cybersecurity competencies. However, as in the scenario, organizations began to understand that competence is not readiness.

We developed the workforce readiness project based on lessons learned from identifying and documenting cybersecurity competencies for client organizations, as well as observations of work performed in related software engineering settings. The project's competency work initially focused solely on cybersecurity. However, over time the project scope broadened to include, for example, supervisors' readiness to perform their assigned leadership duties. 

As we shifted the focus of our research from developing and documenting competencies to building workforce readiness, we leveraged previous SEI work in building readiness using certification programs [Behrens 2004] and cybersecurity workforce development [Hammerstein 2010]. We also looked at relevant research throughout the training and development community. 

In particular, we reviewed materials focused on how to build competency-based training ® CERT and Carnegie Mellon are registered marks owned by Carnegie Mellon University.

Below is a concise, evidence-backed explanation of how “general-workforce digital skills” and “tech-job digital skills” differ, and why certain tech skills migrate from specialized roles into general, cross-domain work over time.

Definitions and categories

General-workforce digital skills are the abilities needed to use, evaluate, and integrate digital tools into everyday tasks across occupations, emphasizing foundational computer use, information processing, problem solving, communication, and security, along with adaptability and collaboration rather than deep systems engineering. <cite id="74386a8e-2">As digitisation spreads to all sectors, most jobs already require basic digital skills and intensive ICT use at work is associated with greater problem solving, interaction with clients and co-workers, less physical work, and higher numeracy</cite>. <cite id="74386a8e-4">OECD distinguishes ICT specialists (develop, operate, maintain ICT systems), advanced users (competent users of sector-specific software), and basic users (generic tools for work life), and highlights growing demand for programming and network skills alongside complementary ICT skills such as information processing, problem solving, and communication, as well as leadership and teamwork</cite>. <cite id="74386a8e-0">O*NET-based analyses show that core skills like critical thinking, problem solving, communication, teamwork, flexibility/adaptability, and creativity are required across broad occupational clusters including software developers and managers</cite>.

Tech-job digital skills, by contrast, denote deeper, domain-specific technical competencies needed to design, implement, operate, and maintain specialized systems (e.g., software development, network/IT operations, data engineering), often with pay premiums and limited transferability when tools or architectures change rapidly. <cite id="599f3ec0-0">ICT and automation research (Autor et al.; Acemoglu & Restrepo) documents how digital technologies co-evolve with task reorganization and skill demand, with ICT-skilled workers earning more and gaining experience with more abstract, less routinized content</cite>. <cite id="599f3ec0-3">Evidence that higher ICT skills are rewarded with higher pay and experience working with more abstract digital content indicates the premium on advanced, tech-specific capabilities</cite>. <cite id="74386a8e-4">OECD further distinguishes these specialist competencies from advanced use and basic use, underscoring that programming, application development, and network management sit at the specialist end</cite>. <cite id="599f3ec0-4">Interviews with creative-industries leaders show a narrow, technical view of digital skills that is limited in flexibility and quickly outdated as technology advances, whereas generic skills like communication and problem solving are repeatedly emphasized</cite>.

Why tech skills migrate into the general workforce

- Ubiquity and diffusion of digital tools lower barriers to entry. <cite id="74386a8e-2">As ICT becomes embedded in routine work, “most jobs already require basic digital skills,” and intensive ICT use changes task content toward problem solving and interaction</cite>. <cite id="74386a8e-3">Digitalisation is not limited to IT jobs or industries; it affects the whole world of work and changes skill requirements of jobs, with demand for ICT-related skills rising and influencing wage differentials</cite>. <cite id="43d7b37b-1">Capabilities demonstrated in coding extend to document processing, financial analysis, and routine administrative tasks, and early organizational adoption has already occurred (e.g., AI in HR, hiring freezes for non-technical roles, projections of 30% of financial tasks automated by 2030)</cite>. <cite id="43d7b37b-2">Digital technologies are widely introduced into different occupations, with computers being the most widespread form of digital work, though implementation varies by task domain</cite>.

- Organizational task reorganization embeds tech into general workflows. <cite id="43d7b37b-0">When plants reorganize after closures, workers with routine-intensive tasks struggle to find comparable jobs at new factories, while those with less routinized learning also face difficulty, indicating that prior learning at older factories did not prepare them for new, digital technologies</cite>. <cite id="43d7b37b-2">Digital technologies are systematically changing job quality, and task-specific influences differ across knowledge work, manufacturing, services; job tasks and technologies co-evolve, often in ways that generalize computer work across roles</cite>. <cite id="43d7b37b-4">Digital transformation in firms increases the intensity of abstract, routine, and manual tasks, with significantly larger effects for abstract tasks, consistent with substitution being offset by complementarities in workflows</cite>. <cite id="74386a8e-3">Employment in jobs related to digital tasks tends to grow faster, and indicators show digital skill requirements changing; task composition shifts as ICT becomes embedded</cite>.

- Complementarity with general-purpose cognitive skills accelerates reuse across roles. <cite id="599f3ec0-1">Self-assessed digital skills correlate with actual skills for operational tasks, suggesting that measured improvements during shocks like COVID-19 reflect gains in routine digital use; however, such skills may be insufficient where deeper capabilities are needed</cite>. <cite id="599f3ec0-3">Workers with higher ICT skills experience more abstract, less routinized content; in a 1982 cohort, taking advanced mathematics predicted better adaptation to technological evolution, higher pay, and greater likelihood of STEM employment</cite>. <cite id="74386a8e-0">Cross-country O*NET evidence shows critical thinking, communication, teamwork, flexibility/adaptability, and creativity are broadly required in clusters spanning software developers and managerial roles, indicating that general-purpose cognitive and social skills pair with digital tools to expand applicability</cite>. <cite id="74386a8e-1">Workforce development should target not only job-specific technical skills but also general skills that support cross-functional learning and mobility, as foundational, structurally embedded capabilities underpin long-term adaptability</cite>. <cite id="599f3ec0-4">A narrow focus on technical operations leads to skills that are quickly outdated; generic skills like communication and problem solving are essential in practice</cite>.

- Rapidly evolving AI and generative tools compress the gap between tech-specific and general tasks. <cite id="43d7b37b-1">AI capabilities demonstrated in coding generalize to document processing, financial analysis, and routine admin; adoption is already displacing roles (e.g., HR) and reconfiguring non-technical hiring, with projections that 30% of financial tasks could be automated by 2030</cite>. <cite id="43d7b37b-0">Even as digital occupations grow, routinized jobs tend to decline, reinforcing the movement of digital capabilities into less-routinized, cross-domain tasks</cite>. <cite id="599f3ec0-3">Experience working with more abstract, advanced digital technologies is associated with higher ICT pay and less routinization, consistent with AI-enabled task elevation</cite>.

Mechanisms observed in practice

- Learning-by-doing across plants and occupations. <cite id="43d7b37b-0">After plant closures, redundant workers’ prior learning did not transfer to new factories with changing digital technologies; routine-intensive workers struggled to find comparable jobs</cite>. <cite id="599f3ec0-3">Experience with abstract content and advanced ICT is rewarded, indicating that on-the-job learning with evolving tools fosters adaptability and cross-occupation mobility</cite>.

- Demand shifts and skill requirement changes. <cite id="599f3ec0-3">Digital occupations grow while routinized employment declines; learning at older, less digitalized factories did not prepare workers for new digital technologies</cite>. <cite id="74386a8e-3">Digital skill requirements across occupations increase and evolve, with ESCO- and survey-based indicators showing that ICT-related skills are rising in demand</cite>. <cite id="43d7b37b-4">Firm-level digital transformation significantly elevates abstract task intensity (β = 0.446) relative to routine (0.248) and manual (0.333), indicating a shift toward problem-solving, non-routine analytical capabilities</cite>.

- Complementary training and facility/uptake. <cite id="599f3ec0-1">Digital skill improvements during lockdowns correlate with operational abilities, but a gap persists between self-assessments and objective tests, suggesting that explicit training is needed for durable gains</cite>. <cite id="599f3ec0-2">In Malaysian services, both facility/training and applied digital skills (hard and soft) significantly correlate with digital skills readiness in the general workforce</cite>. <cite id="74386a8e-4">Policy and sector analyses emphasize pairing specialist and advanced-use competencies with complementary ICT skills (information processing, problem solving, communication) and soft skills (leadership, teamwork), which expand market opportunities</cite>.

Evidence of migration from tech-specific to general categories

- Software and AI capabilities spilling into non-tech domains. <cite id="43d7b37b-1">Tools developed for coding extend to document processing, financial analysis, and routine administrative tasks, with early organizational impacts (e.g., AI in HR, hiring freezes in non-technical roles, projected automation of 30% of financial tasks)</cite>. <cite id="43d7b37b-0">Digital occupation growth coexists with declines in routinized jobs, consistent with tech capabilities being integrated into non-tech workflows</cite>. <cite id="599f3ec0-3">Workers with higher ICT skills are rewarded with experience in more abstract, less routinized content, indicating tech-derived capabilities that generalize across tasks</cite>.

- Task-level changes that embed tech into general roles. <cite id="43d7b37b-4">Digital transformation increases abstract task intensity disproportionately, elevating demand for cognitive flexibility and problem solving—capabilities used across professional, administrative, and managerial roles</cite>. <cite id="74386a8e-2">Across countries, intensive ICT use at work increases problem solving and interaction while reducing physical work, implying that digital tools are integrated into diverse, non-specialist tasks</cite>. <cite id="74386a8e-3">ESCO-based indicators show that digitalisation transforms skill requirements across the whole world of work, not only IT-specific jobs</cite>.

- Organizational narratives and sector evidence. <cite id="599f3ec0-3">Evidence from plant closures shows that learning in less-routinized roles did not translate to new digital technologies, reinforcing that organizations retrain and redesign for integration; digital occupations grow while routinized jobs fall</cite>. <cite id="599f3ec0-4">Leaders in creative industries report that technical digital skills are viewed as a narrow, quickly outdated basis, whereas generic problem solving and communication are essential to apply digital tools in practice</cite>. <cite id="599f3ec0-1">Pandemic-induced digital use improved operational digital skills, but without complementary training and policy attention, gains may remain bounded and uneven across occupations</cite>.

Consequences and strategies

- Pay and mobility: <cite id="599f3ec0-3">ICT-skilled workers earn more and gain experience with more abstract, less routinized content</cite>. <cite id="74386a8e-1">Investing in general skills supports cross-functional learning and mobility, enabling workers to combine domain knowledge with digital tools and adapt across roles</cite>.

- Curriculum and practice: <cite id="74386a8e-4">Policies and sector analyses call for pairing specialist/advanced-use digital skills with complementary ICT and soft skills to expand opportunities</cite>. <cite id="599f3ec0-2">Applied digital readiness rises with both facility/training and hard/soft digital skills, underscoring the value of blended training pathways into general workforce roles</cite>. <cite id="599f3ec0-4">Organizations should avoid equating “technically digital” with “competent,” since technical operations are limited in flexibility and quickly become outdated; explicit development of communication, problem solving, and strategic digital skills broadens applicability</cite>.

- Managerial design: <cite id="43d7b37b-2">Digital technologies change job quality across task domains, implying deliberate task redesign, onboarding, and support to recombine tech tools with general-purpose capabilities</cite>. <cite id="43d7b37b-0">When technologies change, prior learning does not automatically transfer; structured transition and reskilling are needed to move routine workers into higher-abstract, digitalized roles</cite>.

Summary and open questions

In short, general-workforce digital skills are foundational, integrative abilities to use and improve digital tools within broad job tasks (information processing, problem solving, communication), while tech-job digital skills are deeper, domain-specific competencies to design, build, and operate specialized systems. <cite id="74386a8e-4">OECD’s specialist/advanced/basic user distinction and industry 4.0 evidence show how specialist competencies sit alongside complementary general-purpose capabilities in both tech and non-tech roles</cite>. Tech skills migrate into the general workforce when tools become ubiquitous, organizations redesign tasks to embed digital work, and general-purpose cognitive and social skills complement technical depth; these forces are amplified by AI and generative tools that generalize capabilities from coding into document, financial, and administrative work. <cite id="43d7b37b-1">Digital AI capabilities translate across domains with early organizational impacts</cite>, <cite id="43d7b37b-2">computer work is widespread across occupations with varying implementation</cite>, and <cite id="43d7b37b-4">digital transformation elevates abstract, problem-solving task demands</cite>. Persistent gaps arise from uneven training, limited transferability of narrow technical skills, and organizational constraints; policy and managerial attention to blended skill development and task redesign are crucial to sustain durable migration and inclusive adaptability. <cite id="74386a8e-1">Targeting both job-specific technical skills and general, structurally embedded capabilities is essential</cite>, and <cite id="599f3ec0-4">organizations must move beyond a narrow technical conception of digital skill to include strategic, communication, and problem-solving capacities that do not quickly become outdated</cite>.

Second, from a practitioner standpoint, O*NET is a framework used by different OB/OP disciplines and labor stakeholders (e.g., firms, consulting, governments, international organizations), thus allowing the use of a common language in order to analyze the current work with other organizational and practical discussions (Guzzo, 2019;Kanfer & Blivin, 2019). Third, from a methodological view, O*NET is considered as one of the most comprehensive and widely frameworks and tools used to evaluate skill requirements in different cultural contexts, take New Zealand, China, Hong Kong, for instance (Dierdorff & Ellington, 2019).

Title: Unraveling Human Capital Complexity: Economic Complexity Analysis of Occupations and Skills
Snippet: Workforce development and reskilling programs should not only target job-specific technical skills, but also prioritize general skills that support cross-functional learning and mobility. In a labor market increasingly shaped by automation and shifting skill demands, investing in foundational, structurally embedded capabilities is essential for ensuring long-term adaptability and inclusive economic opportunity. Specialized (or specific) skills, which are directly associated with a worker's competency, and general skills, which enhance the resilience of the labor market, are traditionally treated as distinct categories [13,14,15,16]. While general skills have remained relatively overlooked, prior network-based studies of the labor market have often emphasized over-expressed skills within each occupation by normalizing skill importance data [3]. Such normalization is an appropriate approach when identifying the skills a worker needs to be competitive in the labor market. However, this approach tends to render general skills-which contribute widely across the occupations-more implicit by emphasizing the only distinctive features of each occupation.

Title: Online Research for the Impact of ICTs on Greek Women's Employability and Entrepreneurship
Snippet: As digitisation spreads to all sectors of the economy, digital skills are increasingly needed for most jobs. Indeed, most jobs already require basic digital skills. In the future this will only increase and it can be argued that all labour force participants need these skills to remain employable and for entrepreneurship. Despite this, around 37% of the labour force (employed, self-employed and unemployed) in the EU does not have even basic digital skills. The European labour force needs to be re-skilled for its digital future beyond basic digital skills with a view to professional-related digital needs. Special attention should be paid to skills related to security. 

Occupations provide another way of looking at changes in employment. Job losses affect different types of workers in different ways, depending on their skills and the type of tasks carried out on the job. According to the OECD (2015), women in nonroutine and routine-intensive occupations tend to suffer proportionally less during crises and to benefit relatively more during expansions. Among the factors that may contribute to explaining these gender-specific patterns are differences in the distribution of employment of men and women in the public and private sectors, industryand-gender specific dynamics such as the marked decline of construction activities (a male-dominated sector), and the specific type of job accomplished (e.g. personal care). 

The results from the first OECD Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) show large differences in computer use at work across countries. The increasing use of ICTs at work requires workers to perform different tasks and to develop complementary skills. On average, intensive use of ICTs at work iJAC -Vol. 10, No. 1, 2017 is associated with greater interaction between co-workers and clients, more problem solving, less physical work and higher numeracy. For most tasks, correlations with ICTs tend to decrease with the skill level of the occupation. Job recovery is becoming more widespread and gaining momentum with unemployment declining in most countries, including those hardest hit by the crisis (OECD, 2015b). According to OECD statistics (2015), youth employment rates remain of particular concern, especially in Europe, with average unemployment rates for younger workers (15-24 years old) at over 20%, rising to above 40% in Spain, Greece and Italy.

Title: Digitalisation of occupations—Developing an indicator based on digital skill requirements
Snippet: Digitalisation transforms every realm of our society and, in particular, for workplaces, this process has been accelerated by the on-going Covid-19 pandemic. This digital transformation, however, is not limited to specific IT-jobs or industries, but affects the whole world of work. Several studies forecast a replacement of jobs by digital technologies ranging between less than 10 per cent up to more than 50 per cent (e.g. [1][2][3]). While these studies are future-oriented, the work in [4,5] shows that these changes are already taking place in the US labour market. Similarly, the results of [6] suggest that employment in jobs related to digital tasks tends to grow faster in Italy. Overall, these studies indicate that the widespread use of ICT at work changes skill requirements of jobs, and that the demand for ICT-related skills is expected to continue to rise thereby affecting wage differentials between workers with different levels of digital skills [7]. 

Consequently, measuring the digital skill requirements of occupations is highly relevant to inform research and policy makers in the face of societal challenges posed by the digital transformation. With this paper, we therefore aim to provide an indicator to measure the degree of digitalisation based on digital skills using the classification of European Skills, Competences, Qualifications and Occupations (ESCO). 

Thus far, several indicators have been developed to quantify ICT skill requirements of jobs. These indicators typically approximate skills via tasks based on data collected through surveys assessing what workers do at work. Among the surveys most commonly used, we find the OECD 'Programme for the Assessment of Adult Skills' (PIAAC) [8,9], the Italian 'Indagine Campionaria sulle Professioni' (ICP) [6], and the survey data from US Occupational database ONET [4]. 

Occupational indicators derived from survey data, however, suffer from some drawbacks: self-reported tasks are affected by respondents' perception of an occupation and they are therefore subject to survey bias. Most surveys are not updated frequently and are therefore ill-fitted to track changing task compositions. Moreover, surveys cannot go into great detail on the variety and specificity of tasks. Finally, while tasks measure what people do at work, they provide little information on the skills required to perform a task.
</snippet>

The first category of presented competencies covers individuals who supply the tools, while the second and third categories cover those who use them. Recently, it was recognized that the interconnection of the ICT sector with other manufacturing and services sectors implies a greater demand for new skills. Namely;according to OECD 21 this kind of demand is emerging in the areas of programming, application development and network management skills, generic ICT skills for professional purposes and complementary ICT skills to perform new ICT related tasks such as information processing, problem solving and communication. Furthermore, it is assumed that workforce in contemporary (information) society needs different types of skills, such as technical and professional (including ICT professionals who are the heart of innovation and support for digital infrastructure), and complementary ICT or soft-skills, such as leadership and communication skills that expand market opportunities. Title: Digital technologies, innovation, and skills: emerging trajectories and challenges
Snippet: Employing an original dataset on occupations in Italy in the period 2011-2016, they analyze the relationship between digitalization, task routinization, and employment. They find that "digital occupations" (i.e., activities that explicitly involve digital technologies) are not necessarily associated with routinized occupations and that, although employment in digital occupations is growing, jobs in routinized occupations tend to decrease. 

Discussing the challenge of attaining a better understanding of the relationship between the evolution of digital technologies, organization, and skills, Goos, Rademakers, and Röttger (in this issue) analyze data on workers collected before and after a plant closure to examine what happens to redundant workers. They show that workers who engaged in routine-intensive tasks, in contrast to their peers who performed less-routinized tasks, struggled to find employment at new factories. And workers who had less-routinized jobs but worked at older factories could not find jobs of similar quality, suggesting that their learning at an older factory did not prepare them for working with changing (digital) technologies in new factories. 

The question of which skills workers should develop to keep up with increasing digitalization is somewhat vexatious. Two papers in the special issue present significant evidence that is relevant to this question, addressing the challenge of achieving a better understanding of the evolution of digital technologies, organization, and skills, from the perspective of skills. In a cross-country data setting, Falck et al. (in this issue) show that workers with higher ICT skills earn more than their peers with lower ICT skills and gain experience working with more abstract content (i.e., less routinized and using more advanced digital technologies). Further light on these issues is cast by Black et al who use data from a survey of US high school graduates in 1982, at the inception of the digital revolution. They found that the educational experience that was most important in preparing them for a labor market in which they would need to use and learn new digital technologies, was taking courses in advanced mathematics. Those who did so were more likely to find better-paid jobs, better able to adapt to technological evolution, and more likely to be employed in STEM occupations. 

The next paper in the issue addresses the third challenge, the role of digital technologies in the economy and society.

Title: The Iceberg Index: Measuring Skills-centered Exposure in the AI Economy
Snippet: Beyond technology occupations, AI capabilities extend to cognitive and administrative work. Tools developed for coding demonstrate technical capability in document processing, financial analysis, and routine administrative tasks -illustrating how capabilities demonstrated in technology contexts translate to other domains. Some adoption is already occurring: IBM reduced HR staff through AI automation [26], Salesforce froze hiring for non-technical roles [29], and McKinsey projects that 30% of financial tasks could be automated by 2030 [15]. 

We apply the same skill-overlap methodology to administrative, financial, and professional service occupations beyond the technology sector. The Iceberg Index for digital AI shows values averaging 11.7%-five times larger than the 2.2% Surface Index. Unlike technology-sector exposure concentrated in coastal hubs, this broader skill overlap is geographically distributed. South Dakota, North Carolina, and Utah show higher Index values than California or Virginia. 

Industrial states illustrate this pattern. Tennessee (11.6%) and Ohio (11.8%) show substantial Index values driven by administrative and coordination roles within factories and supply chains. These white-collar functions show technical exposure that maybe invisible to policymakers while states focus largely on physical automation. These patterns reveal where skill overlap extends beyond current visible adoption, though actual workforce impacts will depend on adoption decisions, quality thresholds, and organizational constraints (Figure 6(a)).

Title: “Digital Taylorism” for some, “digital self-determination” for others? Inequality in job autonomy across different task domains
Snippet: Thus, digital technologies have been widely introduced into the world of work, although the way in which they are implemented likely varies across job tasks. While the concept of tasks is not uniformly defined across different fields of research, certain task domains, such as knowledge work, manufacturing, service or interactive work, appear in many areas of labour-related research (for a discussion see Autor et al. 2003;Böhle/Glaser 2006;MacDonald/ Korczynski 2009;Spitz-Oener 2006). Increasingly, task-specific influences of digital technology are also being taken into account. This is particularly relevant as, for instance, a computer is used differently depending on whether it is used for knowledge work, manufacturing or simple services. 

Although the link between job tasks and digital technology is already considered in some influential economic approaches (notably the TASK approach, see Autor et al. 2003), potential changes in job quality are hardly considered. Instead, more attention is paid to the interaction between job tasks and technology in terms of future job losses. Here, the occupation-specific probability of job loss is predicted by the composition of different tasks within occupations, distinguishing for example between (non-)routine and (non-)cognitive tasks. However, technologies and related job tasks are changing, in some cases substantially (Dengler/Matthes 2018). Moreover, the dominant debate about future job losses ignores the fact that digital technology is already systematically changing employees' job quality. So far, however, this has only been researched selectively, often looking at a very specific technology. 

One of the main reasons for the lack of comprehensive and generalisable findings is the limited diffusion of new digital technologies, such as various wearables or AI applications. Many of the currently discussed examples are still under develop-ment and their implementation in practice is often limited to a few pioneers. Accordingly, empirical evidence based on large, representative studies is rare. If we abstract from the digital technologies that are currently being intensively discussed but rarely used, it quickly becomes clear that the digital world of work is already in full swing. This is particularly true for computer work, which is currently the most widespread form of digital work and is therefore found in many different occupations.

Title: Using digital traces to analyze software work: skills, careers and programming languages
Snippet: Our findings connect with the literature on skill complexity, labor market transitions, and the organization of work, complementing studies that have emphasized how granular task analysis can reveal hidden dynamics in career mobility, wage disparities, and skill complementarities [Autor et al., 2003, Anderson, 2017, Alabdulkareem et al., 2018, del Rio-Chanona et al., 2021]. Previous research however, tends to use standardized task classifications such as O*NET to define tasks and applies them to curated job descriptions, limiting the granularity and responsiveness of task taxonomies. In contrast, by extracting tasks directly from real-world problem-solving interactions on Stack Overflow, our approach captures the immediate and practical realities of skill application at a global scale. In rapidly changing sectors such as software engineering, tasks derived from activities can explain surprising developments like the rise of the Python programming language as a technology which enables diversification into more valuable tasks. This complements existing work on task-relatedness and collective learning. 

We highlight three possible applications of our method and taxonomy. First we have demonstrated that microdata on activity can be fruitfully aggregated into tasks to describe skill acquisition, development and transitions. Tasks from any sector in which large-scale fine-grained activity on individual behavior at work is available could be categorized in a similar manner. Second, employers in such sectors can use our approach to identify skills related to tasks their employees actually carry out, enabling better labor market matching outcomes or internal skill development programs. Finally, educators can better understand the labor market landscape of the software industry using our taxonomy. 

There are several limitations to our study, which may be tackled in future work. First, we have focused exclusively on programming-related tasks. However, software developers need to be able to carry out many other tasks, such as managing teams or reporting results. Although SO contains some postings about organizational aspects of software development, its emphasis is on technical subjects. To explore how programming tasks are combined with other types of tasks in software jobs, future studies could use job ads to compare the co-occurrence of our programming tasks with tasks related to different kinds of soft skills.
</snippet>

Below is a concise, evidence-backed explanation of how “general-workforce digital skills” and “tech-job digital skills” differ, and why certain tech skills migrate from specialized roles into general, cross-domain work over time.

Definitions and categories

General-workforce digital skills are the abilities needed to use, evaluate, and integrate digital tools into everyday tasks across occupations, emphasizing foundational computer use, information processing, problem solving, communication, and security, along with adaptability and collaboration rather than deep systems engineering. <cite id="74386a8e-2">As digitisation spreads to all sectors, most jobs already require basic digital skills and intensive ICT use at work is associated with greater problem solving, interaction with clients and co-workers, less physical work, and higher numeracy</cite>. <cite id="74386a8e-4">OECD distinguishes ICT specialists (develop, operate, maintain ICT systems), advanced users (competent users of sector-specific software), and basic users (generic tools for work life), and highlights growing demand for programming and network skills alongside complementary ICT skills such as information processing, problem solving, and communication, as well as leadership and teamwork</cite>. <cite id="74386a8e-0">O*NET-based analyses show that core skills like critical thinking, problem solving, communication, teamwork, flexibility/adaptability, and creativity are required across broad occupational clusters including software developers and managers</cite>.

Tech-job digital skills, by contrast, denote deeper, domain-specific technical competencies needed to design, implement, operate, and maintain specialized systems (e.g., software development, network/IT operations, data engineering), often with pay premiums and limited transferability when tools or architectures change rapidly. <cite id="599f3ec0-0">ICT and automation research (Autor et al.; Acemoglu & Restrepo) documents how digital technologies co-evolve with task reorganization and skill demand, with ICT-skilled workers earning more and gaining experience with more abstract, less routinized content</cite>. <cite id="599f3ec0-3">Evidence that higher ICT skills are rewarded with higher pay and experience working with more abstract digital content indicates the premium on advanced, tech-specific capabilities</cite>. <cite id="74386a8e-4">OECD further distinguishes these specialist competencies from advanced use and basic use, underscoring that programming, application development, and network management sit at the specialist end</cite>. <cite id="599f3ec0-4">Interviews with creative-industries leaders show a narrow, technical view of digital skills that is limited in flexibility and quickly outdated as technology advances, whereas generic skills like communication and problem solving are repeatedly emphasized</cite>.

Why tech skills migrate into the general workforce

- Ubiquity and diffusion of digital tools lower barriers to entry. <cite id="74386a8e-2">As ICT becomes embedded in routine work, “most jobs already require basic digital skills,” and intensive ICT use changes task content toward problem solving and interaction</cite>. <cite id="74386a8e-3">Digitalisation is not limited to IT jobs or industries; it affects the whole world of work and changes skill requirements of jobs, with demand for ICT-related skills rising and influencing wage differentials</cite>. <cite id="43d7b37b-1">Capabilities demonstrated in coding extend to document processing, financial analysis, and routine administrative tasks, and early organizational adoption has already occurred (e.g., AI in HR, hiring freezes for non-technical roles, projections of 30% of financial tasks automated by 2030)</cite>. <cite id="43d7b37b-2">Digital technologies are widely introduced into different occupations, with computers being the most widespread form of digital work, though implementation varies by task domain</cite>.

- Organizational task reorganization embeds tech into general workflows. <cite id="43d7b37b-0">When plants reorganize after closures, workers with routine-intensive tasks struggle to find comparable jobs at new factories, while those with less routinized learning also face difficulty, indicating that prior learning at older factories did not prepare them for new, digital technologies</cite>. <cite id="43d7b37b-2">Digital technologies are systematically changing job quality, and task-specific influences differ across knowledge work, manufacturing, services; job tasks and technologies co-evolve, often in ways that generalize computer work across roles</cite>. <cite id="43d7b37b-4">Digital transformation in firms increases the intensity of abstract, routine, and manual tasks, with significantly larger effects for abstract tasks, consistent with substitution being offset by complementarities in workflows</cite>. <cite id="74386a8e-3">Employment in jobs related to digital tasks tends to grow faster, and indicators show digital skill requirements changing; task composition shifts as ICT becomes embedded</cite>.

Mechanisms observed in practice

Consequences and strategies

- Pay and mobility: <cite id="599f3ec0-3">ICT-skilled workers earn more and gain experience with more abstract, less routinized content</cite>. <cite id="74386a8e-1">Investing in general skills supports cross-functional learning and mobility, enabling workers to combine domain knowledge with digital tools and adapt across roles</cite>.

Title: Exploring skill requirements for the Industry 4.0: A worker-oriented approach
Snippet: O*NET is a tool widely used in the scholar and practitioner milieu. By using different descriptors, sub-dimensions or dimensions of this taxonomy, several researchers have conducted studies to analyze skill requirements (e.g., Burrus et al., 2013;Frey & Osborne, 2017). More recently, by using a job-oriented approach and exploiting the O*NET database, Dierdorff and Ellington (2019) conducted a study on six different clusters of skills considered as relevant (i.e., critical thinking and problem solving, communication, teamwork and collaboration, leadership, flexibility and adaptability, creativity) related to different occupational groups. Such finding showed that about 45% of occupations investigated were grouped into two occupational clusters: (1) architecture and engineering occupations (e.g., software developers, electrical engineering technologists) and (2) management and life, physical, and social science occupations (e.g., plant managers, foresters). Two major occupational groups where such skills are more required (i.e., above-average mean importance score). 

In order to identify functional and general groups of skills for the industry 4.0, we used and adapted skills descriptors from O*NET Content Model for three reasons. First, from a theoretical perspective, most of the existing proposals on skills research addresses, in one way or another, the most distinctive theoretical aspects of skills evoked in this comprehensive taxonomy (e.g., Sousa & Wilks, 2018;Kanfer & Blivin, 2019). Second, from a practitioner standpoint, O*NET is a framework used by different OB/OP disciplines and labor stakeholders (e.g., firms, consulting, governments, international organizations), thus allowing the use of a common language in order to analyze the current work with other organizational and practical discussions (Guzzo, 2019;Kanfer & Blivin, 2019). Third, from a methodological view, O*NET is considered as one of the most comprehensive and widely frameworks and tools used to evaluate skill requirements in different cultural contexts, take New Zealand, China, Hong Kong, for instance (Dierdorff & Ellington, 2019).

Title: Unraveling Human Capital Complexity: Economic Complexity Analysis of Occupations and Skills
Snippet: Workforce development and reskilling programs should not only target job-specific technical skills, but also prioritize general skills that support cross-functional learning and mobility. In a labor market increasingly shaped by automation and shifting skill demands, investing in foundational, structurally embedded capabilities is essential for ensuring long-term adaptability and inclusive economic opportunity. Specialized (or specific) skills, which are directly associated with a worker's competency, and general skills, which enhance the resilience of the labor market, are traditionally treated as distinct categories [13,14,15,16]. While general skills have remained relatively overlooked, prior network-based studies of the labor market have often emphasized over-expressed skills within each occupation by normalizing skill importance data [3]. Such normalization is an appropriate approach when identifying the skills a worker needs to be competitive in the labor market. However, this approach tends to render general skills-which contribute widely across the occupations-more implicit by emphasizing the only distinctive features of each occupation.

Title: Online Research for the Impact of ICTs on Greek Women's Employability and Entrepreneurship
Snippet: As digitisation spreads to all sectors of the economy, digital skills are increasingly needed for most jobs. Indeed, most jobs already require basic digital skills. In the future this will only increase and it can be argued that all labour force participants need these skills to remain employable and for entrepreneurship. Despite this, around 37% of the labour force (employed, self-employed and unemployed) in the EU does not have even basic digital skills. The European labour force needs to be re-skilled for its digital future beyond basic digital skills with a view to professional-related digital needs. Special attention should be paid to skills related to security. 

Occupations provide another way of looking at changes in employment.
